items.title: Lesson 4 Focus Question: How do the circuits in a school building keep each room's lights independent and protected?

answer.html: The rooms are wired in parallel, so each room's lights and outlets get the full line voltage and work independently. Fuses, circuit breakers and ground-fault interrupters protect against too much current or leakage. Meters (ammeters in series, voltmeters in parallel) are used to measure currents and voltages.

items.title: Lesson 4, Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question: How does energy get from a wind farm to the lights in your classroom?

answer.html: This lesson shows that power reaches the appliances at the line voltage in parallel circuits, that the wiring's own resistance wastes some energy as heat (𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅), and that safety devices stop dangerous currents. Together with the earlier lessons, this explains how the generator's energy reaches the classroom lamps as a circuit: transported at high voltage, stepped down, and transformed into light and thermal energy.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It? (a): Compare how a fuse works with how a circuit breaker works

answer.html: A fuse is a thin metal strip that melts when the current exceeds its rating, opening the circuit; it must be replaced after it blows. A circuit breaker does the same job with a switch that trips (for example a heated bimetallic strip bends and releases a latch) when the current is too high, and it can be reset. Both react to too much current.

answer.html: No. The heater draws 12.5 A, which is less than the 20-A rating. (A second 1500-W heater on the same circuit would bring the total to 25 A, and the fuse would blow.)

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 30: A workshop's lights dim briefly when a table saw starts. Explain why, using the wiring's resistance

answer.html: Real wires are not perfect conductors, so every wire has some resistance. When the saw starts it draws a large current through the shared supply wires, causing a larger voltage drop across the wire resistance (𝛥𝑉= 𝐼𝑅). The lights then get slightly less of the line voltage, so their power (𝑃= (𝛥𝑉)<sup>2</sup> / 𝑅) falls and they dim.

items.title: 75: Describe three protective features of home wiring: a circuit breaker, a GFCI outlet and a grounded three-prong plug

answer.html: (1) Circuit breaker: a resettable switch that trips when the current is too high, preventing overheated wires. (2) GFCI (ground-fault circuit interrupter): senses a small difference between the currents in the two wires (a sign of leakage through water or a person) and shuts off the current. (3) Three-prong plug: the third prong connects the metal case of an appliance to ground, so if a live wire touches the case the current flows to ground and trips the breaker instead of shocking the user.

items.title: 76 (Critical Thinking): Rearrange the three identical bulbs of Circuit S so that they burn with equal intensity. Is the hybrid arrangement of Circuit S ever equal?

body.html: Identical bulbs are equally bright if each has the same current (series) or the same voltage (parallel), since 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉 with equal 𝑅.

answer.html: There are two ways: (1) all three in series, so each carries the same current and gets 𝑉/ 3; or (2) all three in parallel, so each has the full battery voltage. The hybrid arrangement (one in series with a parallel pair) is not equal for identical bulbs: the single bulb has four times the power of each of the pair.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: How does energy get from a wind farm to the lights in your classroom?

body.html: Energy is carried from the wind farm to the lamps by electric current as electrical energy, at high voltage and low current to limit losses, in a complete circuit. Evidence (from the lessons): 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉 links energy delivery to current and voltage. The line loss is 𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅: for example, a 30 A current in 0.10 𝛺 of wire wastes 90 W, but 15 A wastes only 22.5 W, so power is transmitted at very high voltage and stepped down at substations to 240 V or 120 V. Rooms are wired in parallel so each lamp gets the full voltage. A lamp is a resistor that changes electrical energy into light and thermal energy.

Conservation of charge (junction rule) and of energy (loop rule) mean the energy the generator gives the charges is the energy that the line loss, the wires and the devices use up. Because losses grow as 𝐼<sup>2</sup>, using high voltage lowers the current for the same power and delivers more of the energy to the lights.

answer.html: The evidence supports the claim: generators raise the charges' potential energy, high-voltage low- current lines carry it with small 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 loss, and lamps in parallel circuits transform it into light and heat.

items.title: 3: Claim: Does the bulb obey Ohm's law?

answer.html: No. Over this range the bulb is not ohmic: its resistance is not constant.

items.title: 4: Evidence and reasoning

body.html: (1) The 𝐼 versus 𝛥𝑉 graph is a curve, not a straight line through the origin. (2) The calculated resistances are not constant: they rise from 6.25 Ω to 12.5 Ω, a factor of 2.

Ohm's law says 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼 is constant, which gives a straight line through the origin. Here the current rises less than in proportion to the voltage. More current heats the tungsten filament, and a metal's resistance increases with temperature (Table 1), so the bulb's resistance grows as it brightens. The filament is a conductor whose resistance changes with temperature, so over this range it does not obey Ohm's law.

answer.html: The bulb does not obey Ohm's law: the graph curves and 𝑅 doubles from 6.25 Ω to 12.5 Ω because the filament heats up as the current increases.

items.title: Lesson 4 Focus Question: How are circuits used in your home and school?

answer.html: Homes and schools use parallel circuits (each light or outlet gets the full line voltage and works independently), protected by fuses, circuit breakers and ground-fault interrupters. Series-parallel combinations appear wherever the wiring's own resistance matters, and meters (ammeters and voltmeters) are connected in series and parallel to measure currents and voltages.

items.title: Lesson 4, Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question

answer.html: This lesson shows that power is delivered at the line voltage to appliances wired in parallel, that wiring resistance wastes some energy as heat (𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅), and that safety devices stop dangerous currents. Together with the earlier lessons, this explains how electrical energy from the plant reaches the lamps in your home as a circuit.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It? (a): Compare how a fuse works with how a ground-fault interrupter works

answer.html: A fuse is a thin piece of metal that melts when the current through it exceeds its rating, opening the circuit (overcurrent protection). A GFI uses an electronic circuit to compare the currents in the two wires of an appliance cord; if they differ slightly (because some current is leaking through an unintended path, such as a person or water), it shuts off the current. A fuse reacts to too much current; a GFI reacts to a small current imbalance.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 30: Explain why the wiring has resistance

answer.html: Real wires are not perfect conductors. The moving electrons collide with the atoms of the metal, so every wire has some resistance, which grows with its length (and shrinks with its cross-sectional area). When a second appliance is turned on, the extra current causes a larger voltage drop across this wire resistance, so the first appliance gets slightly less voltage and dims.

items.title: 75: Describe three common safety devices in household wiring

answer.html: (1) Fuse: a metal strip that melts when the current is too high, opening the circuit. (2) Circuit breaker: a switch that automatically trips (a heated bimetallic strip bends and releases a latch) when the current exceeds its threshold, and can be reset. (3) Ground-fault interrupter (GFI): senses a small difference between the currents in the two wires of an appliance cord (a sign of leakage, for example through water or a person) and shuts off the current.

items.title: 76 (Critical Thinking): Rearrange Figure 35 so the three bulbs burn with equal intensity. More than one way?

body.html: Identical bulbs are equally bright if each has the same current (series) or the same voltage (parallel), since the power is 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉 with equal 𝑅.

answer.html: Yes, there are two ways (assuming identical bulbs): (1) connect all three bulbs in series, so each carries the same current and gets 𝑉/ 3; or (2) connect all three in parallel, so each has the full battery voltage and the same current. (Parallel gives much brighter bulbs; series gives equally dim ones.)

items.title: Communicate Technical Information: Pamphlet comparing flexible graphene supercapacitors, flexible batteries, and wireless chargers (open-ended)

question.html: This is a creative product, so here is the content a good pamphlet should present (from the article). Technology Pros Cons Flexible graphene supercapacitors Store energy electrostatically on their surfaces; charge in seconds; survive millions of recharges; can be printed on washable clothing High-quality graphene is expensive and labor-intensive; graphene conducts less well than metals Flexible batteries (spiral- wound metal parts, with a solar cell) Bend without breaking; can recharge from sunlight The solar cell is not yet integrated with the battery; still under development Wireless chargers No plug or cable needed; charge devices in the vicinity Currently slow and expensive; few products available

answer.html: A pamphlet should compare the three on speed of charging, durability, flexibility, cost and maturity, using the table above as its core content.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: How does energy get from the power plant to the lights in your home?

body.html: Energy is carried from the plant to the lamps by electric current as electrical energy, at high voltage and low current to limit losses, in a complete circuit. Evidence (from the lessons): 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉 links energy delivery to current and voltage. The line loss is 𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 (Lesson 2: a 41 A current in 1.4 𝛺 of wire wastes 2400 W), so power is transmitted at very high voltage (above 500, 000 V) and stepped down at substations to 240 V or 120 V. Houses are wired in parallel so each appliance gets full voltage. A lamp is a resistor that changes electrical energy into light and thermal energy.

Conservation of charge (junction rule) and of energy (loop rule) mean the energy the generator gives the charges is the energy the line loss, the wires and the devices use up. Because losses grow as 𝐼<sup>2</sup>, using high voltage lowers the current for the same power and delivers more of the energy to the lights.

answer.html: The evidence supports the claim: generators raise the charges' potential energy, high-voltage low- current lines carry it with small 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 loss, and lamps in parallel circuits at home transform it into light and heat.

items.title: 3: Claim: Does the nichrome wire obey Ohm's law?

answer.html: Yes, to a good approximation: over this range the nichrome wire is nearly ohmic, though its resistance rises slightly at higher voltage.

items.title: 4: Evidence and reasoning

body.html: (1) The 𝐼 versus 𝛥𝑉 graph is nearly a straight line through the origin (𝑅<sup>2</sup> ≈0.999 for a linear fit). (2) The calculated resistances all fall in a narrow range (143 to 161 Ω, a spread of about 12% around the mean). (3) Reversing the voltage reverses the current with nearly the same magnitude, so the resistance does not depend on the direction of the current.

Ohm's law says 𝑅= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝐼 is constant, which gives a straight line through the origin. The data are close to this. The small upward drift in 𝑅 with |𝛥𝑉| (the graph bends slightly toward the voltage axis) is consistent with the wire warming at larger current, since a metal's resistance increases with temperature (Table 1). That is a small departure rather than a different kind of behavior.

answer.html: The nichrome wire approximately obeys Ohm's law: the 𝐼-𝛥𝑉 graph is a nearly straight line through the origin, and 𝑅 stays within about 12% of 151 Ω for both current directions, with a slight rise at higher voltage due to heating.
